title: The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder?
claims: This narrative review frames the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) as a best-practice predictor of training-related injuries: acute load is the recent workload, chronic load is the rolling average of medium-term workload.

In elite cricket fast bowlers, an ACWR ≤0.99 was associated with approximately 4% injury likelihood in the following 7 days, while an ACWR ≥1.5 was associated with a 2–4 times greater injury risk in the subsequent 7 days; similar load spikes were reported in elite rugby league and soccer cohorts.

The review proposes 0.8–1.3 as the training “sweet spot” and ≥1.5 as the “danger zone”, while noting that different sports may have different workload–injury relationships and that applying these recommendations to individual-sport athletes should be performed with caution.

The evidence base is a narrative synthesis of mostly elite team-sport cohorts; non-contact injuries are attributed more to inappropriate programming than to training load per se, and the review notes that under-training may also increase injury risk.
